I'll write a piece about the strange, quiet magic of ordinary moments—the kind that don't make it into highlight reels but somehow constitute most of a life.

---

**The Weight of Small Things**

There is a particular quality of light that comes through a kitchen window at 4:47 in the afternoon in late October. It's not golden, exactly—that word belongs to summer evenings and honey and the particular nostalgia of things already lost. This light is thinner, more honest. It falls across the counter where you've left a half-peeled apple, the brown flesh already oxidizing, and it makes the apple look like something an old master might have painted if old masters had bothered with fruit that was about to turn. The light doesn't flatter. It simply *is*, and in its presence, the apple is revealed as exactly what it is: a small, temporary arrangement of sugar and water and the memory of a tree, now slowly returning to itself.

I think about this light often. I think about how most of what we call living happens in rooms like this, with objects like this, in the company of no one who will ever know we were here. The philosopher Heidegger wrote about *Geworfenheit*, the "thrownness" of human existence—the fact that we find ourselves already in a world we didn't choose, with a body we didn't design, speaking a language we didn't invent. He made it sound grim, this condition of being flung into being. But I've come to think it's the source of something tender. We are thrown, yes, but we are also *caught*. By gravity. By the particular angle of a window. By the fact that someone, somewhere, decided that apples should be this color, this shape, this particular balance of sweet and acid.

I am thirty-four years old, or I will be in March, or I was when I started writing this, and the arithmetic of my own life has begun to feel strange to me. Not in the way people mean when they say "time flies"—that cliché about children growing up, about summers blurring together. I mean something more structural. The way that the number 34 contains within it the number 3 and the number 4, and also, if you look at it in a mirror, something else entirely. The way that I have now lived more years as an adult than I lived as a child, a threshold I crossed without noticing, like wading into a river and only later realizing the current has carried you past the point where you could touch bottom.

My grandmother used to say that the first half of your life is spent acquiring things and the second half is spent getting rid of them. She said this when she was seventy, surrounded by the accumulated evidence of a long life: furniture she'd inherited, furniture she'd bought, furniture she'd built with her own hands in the 1950s, when she and my grandfather had first married and had nothing and made everything. She was not a sentimental woman. She had buried two husbands and a daughter and most of her friends, and she did not speak of these losses with the hushed reverence that the living often demand. She spoke of them the way you might speak of weather: *It rained in March. Your aunt died in March. The azaleas came late that year.* The facts, arranged in sequence, the meaning left for you to find or not find.

I did not understand her then. I was twenty-two, full of the particular arrogance of the young, which is not the arrogance of believing you know everything but the subtler arrogance of believing that everything important is still ahead of you. I thought her house was a museum of the past, a refusal to move forward. Now I live in a small apartment with objects that have their own histories, most of them unknown to me: a chair from a flea market in Providence, a lamp with a shade I sewed myself from fabric I found in a dumpster, a collection of stones that I cannot explain but cannot discard. I am becoming, I realize, the kind of person who keeps things. Not because I am sentimental, but because the alternative—the constant shedding, the perpetual becoming-new—seems exhausting, a kind of violence against the self.

There is a stone on my windowsill right now. It is gray, unremarkable, the size of a robin's egg. I found it on a beach in Maine, in a year I cannot precisely place, during a period of my life that I have tried to forget and cannot entirely. I picked it up because it was warm, impossibly warm, as if it had been sitting in direct sunlight while everything around it remained cool. I have carried it since then, through three apartments, two relationships, one marriage that ended and one that began. It has no value. It means nothing, objectively. But it is *mine* in a way that few things are, because I chose it, in a moment of not-thinking, and it has stayed with me through all the thinking I have done since.

The philosopher Gaston Bachelard wrote about the phenomenology of roundness, about how a rounded object—a stone, an egg, a breast—creates a kind of miniature universe, a space of intimacy and protection. He was interested in how we experience space, how the architecture of our surroundings shapes our inner lives. I think about this when I look at my stone, how its smooth surface seems to contain something, how holding it in my palm creates a circuit between my body and this object that has traveled with me through time. The stone does not remember the beach. It does not remember me. But I remember it, and in that remembering, something is preserved that would otherwise be lost.

I have been thinking a lot about loss lately, though not in the dramatic way that the word usually implies. Not the loss of a person, though I have known that too. I mean the loss of *possibility*, the narrowing of the future that happens so gradually that you don't notice it until you try to imagine a life different from the one you're living and find that you cannot. This is the loss that comes with age, I think, though not exclusively. It comes with commitment, with the choosing of one path and the foreclosure of others. It comes with the accumulation of small decisions that, taken together, constitute a life.

When I was younger, I believed that I would always have the option to change. Not just the option—the *certainty* that change was possible, that the self was infinitely plastic, that I could become anyone I wanted to be if I simply worked hard enough, wanted it badly enough. This belief was not entirely false. I have changed, dramatically, in ways that the younger me would not have predicted or perhaps approved of. But I have also become *more* myself in ways that constrain rather than liberate. I have developed preferences, habits, aversions. I have learned what I can tolerate and what I cannot. I have, in short, become a particular person, and the person I am is not the person I imagined I would be, and the person I imagined I would be is not available to me anymore, has never been available, was always a fiction constructed from longing and incomplete information.

This is not a sad realization, though it can feel like one. There is a freedom in constraint, a strange kind of liberation that comes from knowing your limits. The poet Wallace Stevens wrote about "the death of a father" as a kind of opening, a space created by absence. I think of this often in relation to my own father, who died when I was nineteen, suddenly, in a way that left no time for preparation or goodbye. His death did not make me who I am—I was already becoming someone, the process was already underway—but it did change the shape of that becoming, removed certain possibilities, opened others. I have never known my father as an adult. I have never had the conversation that adult children sometimes have with their parents, the one where you recognize them as people, with their own histories and limitations and secret sorrows. I have only the father of my childhood, frozen in that particular light, and the father I imagine, constructed from stories and silences and the things I learned too late.

My mother is still alive. She is eighty-one, and she lives in the house where I grew up, in a town I left and have never fully returned to. We speak on the phone every Sunday, and our conversations follow a pattern that has become almost ritual: the weather, the neighbors, the small ailments that accumulate with age, the memories that surface unbidden. She tells me about her garden, which she tends with a devotion that borders on the religious. She tells me about the books she's reading, which are always more interesting than the books I'm reading, because she has had more time to develop her taste, to discard the merely good in favor of the truly excellent. She tells me about her dreams, which have become more vivid, more insistent, as she has aged. She does not tell me that she is lonely, though I know she is. She does not tell me that she is afraid, though I know she is. These things are communicated in the spaces between words, in the pauses that last a second too long, in the way she asks about my life with an intensity that suggests she is listening for something she cannot name.

I am afraid of becoming like her, and I am afraid of not becoming like her. This is the double bind of inheritance, the way that we are shaped by the people who shaped us, even in our rebellion against them. I left my hometown at eighteen and did not return for ten years. I told myself that I was escaping, that I was brave, that I was forging a life of my own. And I was, in some ways. But I also carried with me the particular silence of that place, the way that certain things were not spoken of, the way that emotion was expressed through action rather than word. I have spent years learning to speak, to name what I feel, to ask for what I need. I am still learning. The learning does not end.

There is a photograph of me at seven, standing in front of a birthday cake, my face split in a grin that shows too many teeth. I am wearing a shirt with a dinosaur on it, green, with a long neck and tiny arms that seem almost apologetic for their uselessness. I look happy in that photograph, genuinely happy, the kind of happiness that children can access before they learn to perform it, before they understand that happiness is something you are supposed to want. I look at that photograph and I feel a tenderness for that child that borders on grief. He does not know what is coming. He does not know that he will lose people he loves, that he will make choices he cannot undo, that he will become someone he does not entirely recognize. He believes, with the certainty of the very young, that the future is a gift that will keep giving, that time is a resource to be spent rather than a limit to be endured.

I want to tell him something. I want to tell him that it gets better, and that it gets worse, and that these are not opposites but the same thing seen from different angles. I want to tell him that the dinosaur shirt is excellent, that he should wear it as often as possible, that one day he will look for it in a box of old clothes and not find it and feel a small, inexplicable loss. I want to tell him that the cake is delicious, that he should eat every bite, that sugar is not the enemy it will later be made out to be. I want to tell him that he is loved, more than he knows, more than he will ever be able to understand, that love is not a feeling but a structure, something that holds you up when you cannot hold yourself.

But I cannot tell him anything. He is gone, or rather, he is not gone but transformed, the cells of his body replaced many times over, the memories overwritten and rewritten, the person he was becoming no longer accessible except in photographs and stories and the occasional dream where he appears, unchanged, asking me questions I cannot answer. This is the nature of time, I think. Not a river flowing forward but a series of rooms, each one containing the person you were, each one locked behind you as you move through, each one available only in retrospect, in the act of looking back.

I have been reading about memory lately, about how it is not a recording but a reconstruction, how each time we remember something we change it slightly, add a detail here, remove an embarrassment there, until the memory we have is not the memory we had but a new memory of having had a memory. This is not a tragedy, I think. It is a kind of mercy. We are allowed to revise our own histories, to become the heroes of our own stories, to forgive ourselves the things we cannot forgive in others. The philosopher Paul Ricoeur wrote about "narrative identity," the way that we constitute ourselves through the stories we tell about ourselves. We are, in this view, not fixed essences but ongoing projects, autobiographies that are never finished, that change with each reading.

I find this comforting and also slightly terrifying. If I am a story, then I can be edited. If I can be edited, then I am not, finally, myself but a version of myself, one of many possible versions, selected by the needs of the moment. The person I was at twenty is not the person I am now, and the person I am now will not be the person I will be at fifty, and each of these persons is real, is true, is *me* in a way that the others are not. This is the mystery of identity, the way that we persist through change, the way that we are both the same and different, the way that the self is a verb as much as a noun, something we do rather than something we are.

I think about this when I look in the mirror, which I do less often than I used to, which I do with a kind of reluctant curiosity. The face I see is familiar and strange, marked by time in ways I did not choose: a line here, a sag there, the particular quality of skin that comes from decades of expression, of weather, of the small injuries that accumulate and heal and leave their traces. I do not recognize myself, not entirely. I recognize the *idea* of myself, the person I believe I am, the story I tell about who I am and how I came to be. But the face in the mirror is a stranger who shares my name, my history, my memories. It is me, and it is not me, and the space between these two truths is where I live.

There is a woman I loved once, or thought I loved, or loved in the way that we love when we are young and do not yet know the difference between love and longing. Her name was Clara, and she had a way of moving through the world that suggested she was always slightly surprised by it, as if she had expected something else and was making the best of what she found. She collected umbrellas, dozens of them, in every color and pattern, though she lived in a city where it rained perhaps forty days a year. She said that umbrellas were "portable architecture," that they created a small, private space wherever you opened them. She was a architect, or wanted to be, and she saw the world as a series of problems to be solved, spaces to be made habitable, even if only temporarily.

We were together for three years, and I have tried to forget her, and I have tried to remember her, and both efforts have failed in their different ways. What remains is not a coherent narrative but a series of images: her hands, always cold, wrapped around a cup of tea; the sound of her laugh, which started in her throat and ended somewhere in her chest; the way she would stop in the middle of a sentence, distracted by something she saw out the window, and I would wait, patient, for her to return. I loved her, I think, in the way that we love our own potential, the person we might become if we are brave enough, if we are lucky enough, if we are loved enough. She left, or I left, or we left each other, and the leaving was not dramatic, not cinematic, just the gradual accumulation of small disappointments, the recognition that we wanted different things, that our architectures did not fit together.

I have wondered, sometimes, what she is doing now. I have wondered if she thinks of me, if she has umbrellas in her new home, if she has built the life she wanted or a life she can tolerate. I do not look her up. I do not send messages or friend requests or the occasional email that goes unanswered. This is not nobility. It is fear, the fear that she has moved on and I have not, that she is happy and I am not, that the story I tell myself about our relationship is not the story she tells, that we were never as important to each other as we were to ourselves. I let her go, and in letting her go, I kept something of her, a version of her that exists only in my memory, that will change with each recollection, that will eventually become someone I never knew.

This is how love works, I think, or how it ends. Not with a bang but with a slow fade, the colors draining from a photograph left in the sun. We do not stop loving. We love differently, love the memory rather than the person, love the idea of what we had rather than the reality of what we lost. And eventually, if we are lucky, we love someone new, and the new love does not replace the old but exists alongside it, a different frequency on the same spectrum, a different note in the same chord.

I am in love now, or I am learning to be, or I am practicing the motions of love until they become natural. His name is David, and he is kind in a way that I did not know I needed, patient in a way that I did not know I required. He listens, really listens, the way some people breathe, without effort, without the need to formulate a response. He has a laugh that starts in his belly and works its way up, that makes him shake, that makes me want to laugh too, even when I don't understand the joke. He is not perfect. He leaves dishes in the sink, he forgets appointments, he has a temper that flares quickly and subsides just as quickly. But he is *here*, present in a way that I have rarely experienced, and his presence makes the world larger, more possible, more worth the effort of living in.

We have been together for two years, which is not long in the scheme of things, which is long enough to know that this is not a passing phase, that we have chosen each other and continue to choose each other, day by day, in the small decisions that constitute a shared life. We have a cat, a gray tabby with one ear that does not stand up straight, who tolerates us both and occasionally deigns to be affectionate. We have a routine, which sounds dull but is not: coffee in the morning, a walk in the evening, dinner together, the particular silence of two people who do not need to fill the space between them. We have plans, tentative, for a future that may or may not arrive: a trip to Japan, a house with a garden, the possibility of children, which we discuss without deciding, leaving the door open in both directions.

I am happy, I think, in the way that happiness is possible, which is to say, intermittently, with interruptions, with the full knowledge that this happiness is temporary, that it will end or change or become something else that I will also call happiness, differently. I am not happy all the time. No one is, or if they are, they are lying or medicated or dead. But I am happy enough, more often than not, and this is a kind of miracle, a small daily miracle that I do not take for granted, that I try to notice, to mark, to remember.

There is a practice in Buddhism called *metta*, loving-kindness meditation, in which you direct goodwill toward yourself and others, repeating phrases like "May I be happy, may I be healthy, may I be safe, may I live with ease." I have tried this practice and found it difficult, the phrases feeling hollow, the goodwill forced. But I have also found, in moments of genuine connection, in the presence of David or my mother or even the cat, a spontaneous version of this practice, a wish for the well-being of another that arises without intention, without effort, simply because the other is there, because their existence is a gift that I did not earn and cannot repay.

I want to be this kind of person, someone who wishes well for others, who recognizes the miracle of their existence, who does not take for granted the brief time we have together. I want to be someone who leaves things better than she found them, who adds to the world rather than subtracting from it, who is remembered, if she is remembered at all, for her kindness rather than her achievements. This is a modest ambition, I think, but it is also a radical one, in a world that values success, visibility, the accumulation of power and wealth. To be kind is to be vulnerable, to risk rejection, to offer something that may not be returned. It is, in its way, braver than any of the conventional heroisms.

I am writing this at night, in the small hours when the world has gone quiet and I am alone with my thoughts, which are not always friendly but are always *mine*, the particular texture of my consciousness that I have learned to navigate, to survive, to occasionally enjoy. The cat is asleep on the bed, a warm weight at my feet. David is asleep beside me, his breathing slow and regular, the sound of it a kind of music that I have learned to sleep to, to wake to, to orient myself by. Outside, the city continues its endless motion, the cars and the people and the small dramas that play out in apartments and bars and hospital rooms, the births and deaths and the ordinary days that constitute a life.

I do not know what will happen tomorrow, or next year, or in the years after that. I do not know if David and I will last, if we will grow together or apart, if we will become the people we need to be for each other or the people we cannot be. I do not know if I will write anything worth reading, if I will make any difference in the world, if I will be remembered or forgotten. These are the questions that keep me awake, that I turn over in my mind like the stone on my windowsill, smooth and cool and full of something I cannot name.

But I also know this: that I am here, now, in this room, with these people and this cat and this stone and this light that will come tomorrow morning, thin and honest, revealing everything and hiding nothing. That I am alive, which is not a small thing, which is the foundation of everything else. That I have loved and been loved, that I have lost and been lost to, that I have been changed by all of it, made into the person I am, the person I am still becoming.

The apple on the counter has turned brown, entirely now, the flesh soft and sweet and beginning to ferment. I will throw it away, or compost it, or leave it for the birds, who will eat it or not eat it, who do not care about my intentions, who live in a world of immediate need and immediate satisfaction. This is not a metaphor, though I could make it one. It is simply an apple, going back to the earth, completing its small cycle, becoming something else, something new, something that will feed other lives in its turn.

I think about this as I write, about cycles and returns, about the way that nothing is ever lost but only transformed, the way that the person I was is still here, in some form, in the person I am, in the person I will be. The child with the dinosaur shirt is not gone. He is in my hands, which have held a thousand things since, in my voice, which still laughs the way his did, in my capacity for wonder, which I have tried to protect, to cultivate, to keep alive against the erosion of time.

Tomorrow I will wake up, and the light will come through the window, and I will make coffee, and I will kiss David, and I will go to work, and I will do the small things that constitute a life, the things that no one will remember but that will add up, that will make the difference between a life that was lived and a life that was merely endured. I will try to be kind. I will try to be present. I will try to notice the light, the stone, the apple, the particular quality of ordinary moments that make up the substance of a life.

This is all I can do. This is enough.

---

*For David, who is asleep beside me, and for everyone who has ever loved me, even briefly, even imperfectly, even in ways I did not understand at the time.*

I want to tell him that the cake is delicious, that he should eat every bite, that sugar is not the enemy it will later be made out to be. I want to tell him that he is loved, more than he knows, more than he will ever be able to understand, that love is not a feeling but a structure, something that holds you up when you cannot hold yourself.

But I cannot tell him anything. He is gone, or rather, he is not gone but transformed, the cells of his body replaced many times over, the memories overwritten and rewritten, the person he was becoming no longer accessible except in photographs and stories and the occasional dream where he appears, unchanged, asking me questions I cannot answer. This is the nature of time, I think. Not a river flowing forward but a series of rooms, each one containing the person you were, each one locked behind you as you move through, each one available only in retrospect, in the act of looking back.

I have been reading about memory lately, about how it is not a recording but a reconstruction, how each time we remember something we change it slightly, add a detail here, remove an embarrassment there, until the memory we have is not the memory we had but a new memory of having had a memory. This is not a tragedy, I think. It is a kind of mercy. We are allowed to revise our own histories, to become the heroes of our own stories, to forgive ourselves the things we cannot forgive in others. The philosopher Paul Ricoeur wrote about "narrative identity," the way that we constitute ourselves through the stories we tell about ourselves. We are, in this view, not fixed essences but ongoing projects, autobiographies that are never finished, that change with each reading.

I find this comforting and also slightly terrifying. If I am a story, then I can be edited. If I can be edited, then I am not, finally, myself but a version of myself, one of many possible versions, selected by the needs of the moment. The person I was at twenty is not the person I am now, and the person I am now will not be the person I will be at fifty, and each of these persons is real, is true, is *me* in a way that the others are not. This is the mystery of identity, the way that we persist through change, the way that we are both the same and different, the way that the self is a verb as much as a noun, something we do rather than something we are.

I think about this when I look in the mirror, which I do less often than I used to, which I do with a kind of reluctant curiosity. The face I see is familiar and strange, marked by time in ways I did not choose: a line here, a sag there, the particular quality of skin that comes from decades of expression, of weather, of the small injuries that accumulate and heal and leave their traces. I do not recognize myself, not entirely. I recognize the *idea* of myself, the person I believe I am, the story I tell about who I am and how I came to be. But the face in the mirror is a stranger who shares my name, my history, my memories. It is me, and it is not me, and the space between these two truths is where I live.

There is a woman I loved once, or thought I loved, or loved in the way that we love when we are young and do not yet know the difference between love and longing. Her name was Clara, and she had a way of moving through the world that suggested she was always slightly surprised by it, as if she had expected something else and was making the best of what she found. She collected umbrellas, dozens of them, in every color and pattern, though she lived in a city where it rained perhaps forty days a year. She said that umbrellas were "portable architecture," that they created a small, private space wherever you opened them. She was a architect, or wanted to be, and she saw the world as a series of problems to be solved, spaces to be made habitable, even if only temporarily.

We were together for three years, and I have tried to forget her, and I have tried to remember her, and both efforts have failed in their different ways. What remains is not a coherent narrative but a series of images: her hands, always cold, wrapped around a cup of tea; the sound of her laugh, which started in her throat and ended somewhere in her chest; the way she would stop in the middle of a sentence, distracted by something she saw out the window, and I would wait, patient, for her to return. I loved her, I think, in the way that we love our own potential, the person we might become if we are brave enough, if we are lucky enough, if we are loved enough. She left, or I left, or we left each other, and the leaving was not dramatic, not cinematic, just the gradual accumulation of small disappointments, the recognition that we wanted different things, that our architectures did not fit together.

I have wondered, sometimes, what she is doing now. I have wondered if she thinks of me, if she has umbrellas in her new home, if she has built the life she wanted or a life she can tolerate. I do not look her up. I do not send messages or friend requests or the occasional email that goes unanswered. This is not nobility. It is fear, the fear that she has moved on and I have not, that she is happy and I am not, that the story I tell myself about our relationship is not the story she tells, that we were never as important to each other as we were to ourselves. I let her go, and in letting her go, I kept something of her, a version of her that exists only in my memory, that will change with each recollection, that will eventually become someone I never knew.

This is how love works, I think, or how it ends. Not with a bang but with a slow fade, the colors draining from a photograph left in the sun. We do not stop loving. We love differently, love the memory rather than the person, love the idea of what we had rather than the reality of what we lost. And eventually, if we are lucky, we love someone new, and the new love does not replace the old but exists alongside it, a different frequency on the same spectrum, a different note in the same chord.

I am in love now, or I am learning to be, or I am practicing the motions of love until they become natural. His name is David, and he is kind in a way that I did not know I needed, patient in a way that I did not know I required. He listens, really listens, the way some people breathe, without effort, without the need to formulate a response. He has a laugh that starts in his belly and works its way up, that makes him shake, that makes me want to laugh too, even when I don't understand the joke. He is not perfect. He leaves dishes in the sink, he forgets appointments, he has a temper that flares quickly and subsides just as quickly. But he is *here*, present in a way that I have rarely experienced, and his presence makes the world larger, more possible, more worth the effort of living in.

We have been together for two years, which is not long in the scheme of things, which is long enough to know that this is not a passing phase, that we have chosen each other and continue to choose each other, day by day, in the small decisions that constitute a shared life. We have a cat, a gray tabby with one ear that does not stand up straight, who tolerates us both and occasionally deigns to be affectionate. We have a routine, which sounds dull but is not: coffee in the morning, a walk in the evening, dinner together, the particular silence of two people who do not need to fill the space between them. We have plans, tentative, for a future that may or may not arrive: a trip to Japan, a house with a garden, the possibility of children, which we discuss without deciding, leaving the door open in both directions.

I am happy, I think, in the way that happiness is possible, which is to say, intermittently, with interruptions, with the full knowledge that this happiness is temporary, that it will end or change or become something else that I will also call happiness, differently. I am not happy all the time. No one is, or if they are, they are lying or medicated or dead. But I am happy enough, more often than not, and this is a kind of miracle, a small daily miracle that I do not take for granted, that I try to notice, to mark, to remember.

There is a practice in Buddhism called *metta*, loving-kindness meditation, in which you direct goodwill toward yourself and others, repeating phrases like "May I be happy, may I be healthy, may I be safe, may I live with ease." I have tried this practice and found it difficult, the phrases feeling hollow, the goodwill forced. But I have also found, in moments of genuine connection, in the presence of David or my mother or even the cat, a spontaneous version of this practice, a wish for the well-being of another that arises without intention, without effort, simply because the other is there, because their existence is a gift that I did not earn and cannot repay.

I want to be this kind of person, someone who wishes well for others, who recognizes the miracle of their existence, who does not take for granted the brief time we have together. I want to be someone who leaves things better than she found them, who adds to the world rather than subtracting from it, who is remembered, if she is remembered at all, for her kindness rather than her achievements. This is a modest ambition, I think, but it is also a radical one, in a world that values success, visibility, the accumulation of power and wealth. To be kind is to be vulnerable, to risk rejection, to offer something that may not be returned. It is, in its way, braver than any of the conventional heroisms.

I am writing this at night, in the small hours when the world has gone quiet and I am alone with my thoughts, which are not always friendly but are always *mine*, the particular texture of my consciousness that I have learned to navigate, to survive, to occasionally enjoy. The cat is asleep on the bed, a warm weight at my feet. David is asleep beside me, his breathing slow and regular, the sound of it a kind of music that I have learned to sleep to, to wake to, to orient myself by. Outside, the city continues its endless motion, the cars and the people and the small dramas that play out in apartments and bars and hospital rooms, the births and deaths and the ordinary days that constitute a life.

I do not know what will happen tomorrow, or next year, or in the years after that. I do not know if David and I will last, if we will grow together or apart, if we will become the people we need to be for each other or the people we cannot be. I do not know if I will write anything worth reading, if I will make any difference in the world, if I will be remembered or forgotten. These are the questions that keep me awake, that I turn over in my mind like the stone on my windowsill, smooth and cool and full of something I cannot name.

But I also know this: that I am here, now, in this room, with these people and this cat and this stone and this light that will come tomorrow morning, thin and honest, revealing everything and hiding nothing. That I am alive, which is not a small thing, which is the foundation of everything else. That I have loved and been loved, that I have lost and been lost to, that I have been changed by all of it, made into the person I am, the person I am still becoming.

The apple on the counter has turned brown, entirely now, the flesh soft and sweet and beginning to ferment. I will throw it away, or compost it, or leave it for the birds, who will eat it or not eat it, who do not care about my intentions, who live in a world of immediate need and immediate satisfaction. This is not a metaphor, though I could make it one. It is simply an apple, going back to the earth, completing its small cycle, becoming something else, something new, something that will feed other lives in its turn.

I think about this as I write, about cycles and returns, about the way that nothing is ever lost but only transformed, the way that the person I was is still here, in some form, in the person I am, in the person I will be. The child with the dinosaur shirt is not gone. He is in my hands, which have held a thousand things since, in my voice, which still laughs the way his did, in my capacity for wonder, which I have tried to protect, to cultivate, to keep alive against the erosion of time.

Tomorrow I will wake up, and the light will come through the window, and I will make coffee, and I will kiss David, and I will go to work, and I will do the small things that constitute a life, the things that no one will remember but that will add up, that will make the difference between a life that was lived and a life that was merely endured. I will try to be kind. I will try to be present. I will try to notice the light, the stone, the apple, the particular quality of ordinary moments that make up the substance of a life.

This is all I can do. This is enough.

---

*For David, who is asleep beside me, and for everyone who has ever loved me, even briefly, even imperfectly, even in ways I did not understand at the time.*
